Specifically, the anti-correlation between [O III]$\lambda5007$/narrow H$β$ and accretion rate is stronger under the Gaussians scheme with a Spearman rank correlation coefficient $r_{\rm s}=-0.412$, than under the Lorentzian scheme with $r_{\rm s}=-0.206$; the same tendency is observed in the narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies (NLS1s) subset ($r_{\rm s}=-0.435$ and $-0.259$ for the Gaussians and Lorentzian schemes, respectively), suggesting that the Gaussians scheme may provide a more self-consistent separation of the broad and narrow H$β$ components. Moreover, the consistent correlations recovered under both profile prescriptions favor a continuous type 1 accretion-state sequence, with NLS1s occupying its high-accretion end rather than constituting a distinct population.

2610.11813.title: The Hand of God Revisited: Revealing the Shell Structure and Jet-Supernova Remnant Interaction in MSH 15-52
2610.11813.abstract: We present an X-ray analysis of the supernova remnant (SNR) MSH 15-52 associated with the young rotation-powered pulsar PSR B1509-58, using Chandra, XMM-Newton, and eROSITA, complemented by MeerKAT radio data. We report the discovery of the missing southern counterpart to the bright northern RCW 89 region and identify a foreground X-ray source that may be a previously unidentified SNR candidate. Imaging and spectroscopy with XMM-Newton and eROSITA reveal the shell properties of MSH 15-52 and suggest that both the southern and northern shell-like structures are consistent with shocked interstellar medium associated with the forward shock, while their low ionization timescales and possible hard power-law components indicate possible influence from particle injection or additional heating by the pulsar wind nebula (PWN) jets. New Chandra spectral maps of the southern jet reveal a region of hard non-thermal emission, with a photon index of approximately 1.6, suggesting interaction between the PWN and the reverse shock and possible re-acceleration of the pulsar outflow. Spatially resolved spectroscopy of the RCW 89 northern clumps reveals high-velocity, metal-rich ejecta with enhanced Ne and Mg abundances. Comparison with core-collapse nucleosynthesis models favors a massive progenitor with an initial mass of approximately 29 solar masses in one-dimensional yield models, while asymmetric explosion models show that lower-mass progenitors can also reproduce the observed abundance ratios. Our study supports a picture in which RCW 89 is part of a larger asymmetric SNR shell interacting with energetic pulsar jets, making the system a valuable laboratory for probing pulsar-PWN-SNR interaction.

2610.13742.title: A strategy for astrometric quasar selection with Gaia DR3 and its application to discover new luminous $z>2$ quasars
2610.13742.abstract: We aim to provide a cookbook for purely astrometric selection of quasars with Gaia DR3 and to provide an example of its use for the identification of very luminous $z>2$ quasars. We analyse the Gaia DR3 astrometry of confirmed quasars and stationary sources. We show that the proper motion signal to noise $μ/σ_μ$ follows a Rayleigh-like distribution. We also show the importance of properly taking into account the correlation between proper motions in right ascension and declination, as well as the non-linear error propagation. We adopt the Mahalanobis distance to the null proper-motion hypothesis. A scaled $χ^2$ distribution with $k=2$ and scale $s=1.1485$ is fitted to Gaia-CRF3; the corresponding $\pm2σ$ Gaussian-equivalent threshold is $D^2_{M(μ)}<7.097$. The final criteria combine this with the parallax condition and $\mathrm{ruwe}<1.4$. Applying the new criteria to the SDSS DR16Q confirmed quasars, the recovery rate is $90.25\%$. The suggested purely astrometric selection significantly improves both completeness and purity compared to other strategies used in the literature, reaching a quasar purity of approximately $95\%$ ($\sim2σ$ Gaussian-equivalent). It can be used to improve the selection purity and completeness for future quasar surveys. As an example, we use the suggested strategi to locate 24 very bright $z>2$ quasars without redshifts in the literature. Our proposed astrometric selection strategy recovers 95\% of known quasars. Its potential use for new discoveries is demonstrated by the identification of 24 very luminous $z>2$ quasars. Ten of these are new discoveries and for an additional seven we correct the redshifts determined by other methods.}

2610.11192.title: Implications of tachyonic phase transition in classically scale invariant general $U(1)_{X}$ models
2610.11192.abstract: We investigate the complementarity between collider searches and gravitational-wave (GW) observations in the classically scale-invariant general $U(1)_X$ extension of the Standard Model. The $U(1)_X$ scale is generated radiatively through the Coleman-Weinberg mechanism, while the electroweak scale is induced through the Higgs portal, without explicit mass terms in the scalar potential. Three right-handed neutrinos are introduced to ensure anomaly cancellation and acquire Majorana masses upon $U(1)_X$ symmetry breaking, which also generates the mass of the neutral gauge boson $Z'$. In the strongly supercooled regime, a tachyonic $U(1)_X$ phase transition can produce a stochastic GW background. Assuming three heavy Majorana neutrinos, we study their effects on the phase-transition dynamics and reheating, and estimate the resulting GW signals. We identify the regions of the $U(1)_X$ gauge coupling and $Z'$ mass accessible to future GW observatories, including LISA and DECIGO, and compare them with existing LEP and LHC constraints. We find that GWs from tachyonic phase transitions can probe regions with small gauge couplings and heavy $Z'$ bosons that are difficult to access through collider searches, demonstrating the complementarity of these probes.

2610.11463.title: Pseudo Closed-Loop Bootstrapping for Reinforcement Learning Based AO Control
2610.11463.abstract: High contrast imaging with ground-based telescopes requires extremely precise wavefront control. The performance of the controller ultimately depends on the quality and efficiency of the wavefront sensing technique, which has led to the development of ever more sensitive wavefront sensors (WFS). However, the increase in sensitivity comes at the cost of greater nonlinearity, which poses challenges for conventional linear reconstructors and controllers. Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a branch of machine learning in which control policies are learned by interacting with the environment. RL has recently attracted interest in the field of XAO, and previous studies have demonstrated that a model-based RL variant, the Policy Optimization for Adaptive Optics (PO4AO), can effectively compensate for temporal delays, misregistration errors, and moderate WFS nonlinearities. PO4AO learns an initial control strategy by collecting closed-loop data from the integrator controller with a linear reconstructor. However, in cases of highly non-linear WFS and challenging conditions, closing the loop with the integrator is difficult, and high-fidelity data cannot be collected. Consequently, learning robust control with PO4AO is challenging. We propose a robust learning strategy in which PO4AO is pre-calibrated using an internal light source and a DM, enabling direct on-sky closed-loop operation without a stable integrator controller for bootstrapping the initial models.

2610.12743.title: Predicted state-to-state collisional rate coefficients from neural networks
2610.12743.abstract: Molecular spectra observed in the interstellar medium are commonly analyzed using non-local thermodynamic equilibrium models, which requires accurate state-to-state collisional rate coefficients. Close-coupling calculations become prohibitively expensive for transitions from highly excited rotational states, therefore available datasets are often truncated at low initial states and temperatures; and since each new system also requires an accurate ab initio potential energy surface, many detected molecules have no collisional data. We employ two machine learning strategies to predict rotational state-to-state rate coefficients of molecules included in the train set beyond the range of initial states and temperatures computed so far, and predicting those of a molecule absent from training and validation sets. Feed-forward neural networks are trained on state-to-state de-excitation rate coefficients of 24 linear molecules colliding with para-H2. Scheme 1 includes all systems in the train+validation set, with 70%, 80%, and 90% initial-state boundaries and a 90% temperature boundary. Scheme 2 is trained on 22 systems described only by transition and molecular properties, and predicts two excluded systems, CS and CF+, whose astrophysical impact is explored with non-LTE calculations. For the 90% boundary, Scheme 1 predicts 99.4% of the test transitions within a factor of 2, and no prediction deviates from the reference value by more than a factor of 4.7. This model was used to complete 18 datasets. Scheme 2 reproduces the rate coefficients of two excluded systems within a factor of 3 for more than 92% of their transitions. Both schemes provide near-instantaneous complements to close-coupling calculations: Scheme 1 extends the range of a molecule already included in the training set with high accuracy, while Scheme 2 gives a reasonable first estimate for a molecule that has not been studied.

2610.14174.title: Searching for Nearby Supermassive Black Hole Binaries with GRAVITY
2610.14174.abstract: We present a systematic interferometric search for close supermassive black hole (SMBH) binaries in 20 nearby type 1 active galactic nuclei (AGN) observed with VLTI/\grav. We investigate parsec-scale asymmetric emission by modeling the squared visibilities and closure phases with a single circular Gaussian component plus a background point source for the central AGN, and searching for additional compact companions through grid-based binary models. The robustness of the search is validated using injection-recovery simulations and point-spread-function diagnostics. Several features are identified in the initial significance maps, but only one candidate out of 20 shows a persistent compact asymmetry, corresponding to an observed incidence of $5\%$. If NGC~3783 is interpreted as a binary AGN, we derive a Poissonian one-sided $1σ$ upper limit of $f_{\rm bin}<16.5\%$ for GRAVITY-detectable binaries among bright nearby AGN (K<12.5) at separations of $\sim1$-$100$~pc. Conversely, if the observed asymmetry in NGC~3783 is associated with asymmetric circumnuclear dust emission, the corresponding upper limit on the binary fraction is $f_{\rm bin}<9.2\%$. We compare these results with predictions from the Horizon-AGN simulation, finding comparable binary fractions. We also noted that the expected fraction strongly depends on the assumed distribution of individual SMBH accretion rates within binaries, which is currently unresolved in cosmological models. Our results demonstrate the potential of infrared interferometry to identify parsec-scale binary AGN candidates and motivate future GRAVITY+ observations to expand the sample and follow up known candidates, helping to confirm their nature and distinguish genuine binaries from asymmetric nuclear structures.

2610.11052.title: Accounting for detector calibration uncertainty in black-hole ringdown analysis
2610.11052.abstract: Detector calibration systematics can bias measurements of a remnant black hole's mass and spin, producing spurious evidence against general relativity if unaccounted for. The ringdown phase in the gravitational-wave signal produced by a binary black-hole merger encodes the remnant properties: at sufficiently late times, the signal is well described by a superposition of quasinormal modes, each with a frequency and damping time set only by the remnant mass and spin. Here we present two complementary approaches for analyzing the ringdown portion of the data to estimate the remnant mass and spin in the presence of a nonnegligible detector calibration error, using the quasinormal-mode rational filter (QNMRF). With a well-measured error, we apply the best-estimated calibration correction to the strain before conducting the standard analysis; with an unknown error, we instead jointly sample the remnant mass, spin and the frequency-dependent calibration error, marginalizing over an uncertainty prior. By injecting the numerical-relativity waveform SXS:BBH:0305 into colored detector noise, at a full-signal matched-filter signal-to-noise ratio of $\sim60$ and with simulated calibration errors of $\pm25\%$ in magnitude and $\pm25^\circ$ in phase, marginalizing over the calibration uncertainty recovers the true mass and spin within the 90\% credible interval, whereas the estimated values are biased if the calibration errors are ignored. We apply the method to GW250207, an event recorded while the Hanford detector response was not well characterized, and recover a remnant consistent with the inspiral-merger-ringdown prediction using the ringdown portion alone, both by correcting for a best-estimated calibration error and by marginalizing over a broad uncertainty prior.

2610.13384.title: Flip-Flop Shocks and Tori in Bondi-Hoyle-Lyttleton Accretion onto Rotating Kerr-Weyl Black Holes and Their Quasi-Periodic Variability
2610.13384.abstract: We present GRHD simulations of Bondi-Hoyle-Lyttleton accretion onto a rotating black hole in Weyl conformal gravity, described by the Kerr-Weyl metric. The equatorial flow is evolved for spins a=0.9M and a=0.5M and several Weyl coefficients, which enter through an effective curvature parameter k, and is compared with Kerr runs sharing the same setup. For the k considered, the horizon, ISCO and test-particle frequencies differ from Kerr by at most ~2%. However, the curvature term grows as kr^2 and acts at the accretion radius R_acc. The flow is controlled by one quantity, eta=|k|R_acc^3/M, the ratio of curvature-induced to Newtonian acceleration at R_acc. For eta<~0.03 a stable shock cone forms, indistinguishable from Kerr. For eta~0.2-0.3 the anti-de Sitter-like term traps shocked gas behind the black hole and drives persistent flip-flop oscillations. For eta>~1.6 the cone is destroyed and an oscillating torus forms. Spin modifies only the inner few gravitational radii and does not change the regime. In strongly deviating models the mean accretion rate is 1.7-3 times the Kerr value and varies by 20-60% rms, versus 0.1-1% in Kerr-like flows. The power spectra show global QPOs with fundamentals at 2.9-4.8 Hz for a 10 Msun black hole, with harmonic ladders whose 3:2 and 2:1 ratios come from one non-sinusoidal oscillation, not resonances. These lie in the low-frequency QPO band and are unrelated to test-particle frequencies (~70-200 Hz). They scale as f_0=xi f_K(R_acc), with xi~0.7-1.1 for stable cones and xi~0.23-0.38 for flip-flop and torus regimes. Strong oscillations would be detectable within seconds for a bright Galactic source. The required |k| exceeds galactic-rotation-curve values by 18-36 orders of magnitude, so a detected shock-driven QPO would measure a local deviation from Kerr, and its absence would constrain |k|.

2610.13183.title: Simulation Study of Reconstruction of Cosmic Ray Extensive Air Shower with Thermal Neutron Detected by ENDA
2610.13183.abstract: In the investigation of the "knee" region within the cosmic ray energy spectrum, extensive air shower (EAS) reconstruction by using different EAS secondary particles are of paramount importance for energy determination and composition separation and finally measurement of energy spectrum of different cosmic ray composition. The Electron-Neutron Detector Array (ENDA) is designed to detect thermal neutrons generated in the ground by high energy hadrons which constitute the "backbone" of EAS and carry vital information regarding the primary cosmic rays. At present, ENDA-64, consisting of 64 detectors, is employed inside the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO). This work simulates the response of ENDA and investigates the lateral distributions of thermal neutrons. A comparison of the NKG and double-exponential functions for describing this distribution using MC simulation data shows that the double-exponential function is more accurate. The mean difference between fitted and measured thermal neutron density is within ~ 6%. Meanwhile, the thermal neutron density at 10 m from the shower axis, $ρ_n$, depends mainly on the sum of all hadrons energy or the number of high-energy hadrons. The relationship between $ρ_n$ and EAS hadron energy or the number of high-energy hadrons can be well fitted by a linear function on a log scale. This work is fundamental for energy determination and composition separation with hybrid detection by using ENDA in the near future.

2610.12880.title: Decomposing the Kinematics of SNR G180.0-01.7 with Medium-Resolution Spectra
2610.12880.abstract: The exceptionally large angular diameter and intrinsic optical faintness of the Galactic supernova remnant (SNR) G180.0-01.7 (S147) have historically hindered a comprehensive spectroscopic census of its filamentary structure. We present the first dedicated medium-resolution (R ~ 7500) spectroscopic study of S147 using the LAMOST Medium-Resolution Spectroscopic survey of Galactic Nebulae (MRS-N). By implementing multi-Gaussian decomposition on the H$α$, [NII], and [SII] emission complexes and applying combined spectroscopic and spatial criteria, we disentangle the shock-ionized filaments of the SNR from the pervasive foreground and background Diffuse Ionized Gas (DIG). Our analysis reveals a distinct bimodal radial velocity distribution for the SNR: a low-velocity population tracing the decelerated forward shock at a dense cavity wall, and a high-velocity population (with absolute radial velocities of ~ 70 $\pm$ 30 km/s) corresponding to ejecta within a low-density cavity. The co-existence of these populations provides kinematic evidence for the "supernova-in-a-cavity" scenario. Furthermore, we detect enhanced [SII]/H$α$ ratios in the DIG along the eastern and northern boundaries of the remnant, signaling shock compression of the ambient interstellar medium and highlighting remnant's multifaceted feedback.

2610.13719.title: High Resolution Spectro-Polarimetric Observations of the Optical Filaments surrounding NGC 1275 with ESPaDOnS
2610.13719.abstract: We analyze archival high spectral resolution ESPaDOnS spectropolarimetric observations (R = $λ/Δλ$ = 68000) of three targeted locations within the filamentary nebula surrounding NGC 1275. We present here the analysis of the main filaments emission lines, namely: [NII]$\lambda6584$, H$α$, and [NII]$\lambda6548$, across our three pointings displaying clear detectable emission, with one also showing additional [SII]$\lambda6716$ and [SII]$\lambda6731$ emission line doublet. Using a Markov Chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC) algorithm and thanks to the exceptionally high spectral resolution of the observations, we resolve for the first time each of the emission lines within one of the pointings into a set of three emission components with a remarkable velocity dispersion contrast ($σ_1 \sim 25$ km/s, $σ_2 \sim 90$ km/s and $σ_3 \sim 208$ km/s). We also perform flux ratios of the three detected emission components, which reveal differences in electron density and ionization sources. Consequently, the ESPaDOnS observations appear to reveal for the first time the overlap of an outer quiescent filament and a central turbulent filament likely affected by the AGN activity at a distance of $\sim 6.8''$ ($\sim 2.5$ kpc) from the central BCG. Finally, ESPaDOnS polarimetric data of one of the pointing allows us to confirm an average linear polarization degree of $\sim 0.15-0.14\%$ and an angle of polarization of $5.3\pm25.7^\circ$ for the optical emission of the filaments, as well as polarization dips associated with the H$α$ emission line and its multiple emission components. We interpret these features and measurements as tentative polarization due to dust scattering.

2610.12308.title: Opening the Black Box: What Neural Networks Learn from Pulsar Timing Array Data
2610.12308.abstract: In recent years, simulation-based inference (SBI) methods have been proposed to address several data-analysis challenges faced by existing and planned gravitational-wave experiments. For example, SBI classification has recently been shown to significantly improve the prospects for detecting anisotropies in pulsar timing array (PTA) data. In this work, we use a simple toy model of a PTA to provide a more pedagogical explanation of how, and under which circumstances, SBI-based detection can improve on classical detection statistics for gravitational-wave background anisotropies.

2610.14119.title: Ultralight scalars and invisible gravitons
2610.14119.abstract: Unless the tensor to scalar ratio is small enough, the non-adiabatic mode associated with the ultralight bosons may be dangerously comparable with the adiabatic spectrum of curvature inhomogeneities. We point out here that this statement depends on the timeline of the post-inflationary expansion rate. Provided the decelerated evolution is slower than radiation for a sufficiently long period, the relative weight of the non-adiabatic and adiabatic components does not conflict with the direct constraints coming from the large-scale observations. Conversely the presence of ultralight bosons excludes the presence of long stages expanding faster than radiation. The synthesis of the light nuclei and the spectrum of the relic gravitons at high frequencies set the relevant constraints on the duration of the decelerated stages, on the delayed dominance of radiation and on the mass range of the ultralight scalars.

2610.13620.title: Magnetic connectivity from the Sun to the Earth with MHD models II. Impact of input magnetic maps
2610.13620.abstract: Connectivity estimation needs to be fast and thus usually relies on semi-empirical models. We previously established that optimised magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) models can also be used to derive magnetic connectivity, yielding good results, especially for complex configurations. However, the modelling is not the only factor that can impact the connectivity estimation. Models' results, both semi-empirical and MHD, depend heavily on the input data used to drive the simulation. In order to quantify this impact on our connectivity estimation, we used 20 different maps by four providers. We selected the period of July 2019, which corresponds to Carrington rotation (CR) number 2219, because it had already been studied in a previous paper. It corresponds to a period of minimum activity, meaning minimal interference from transient structures, but with a high-speed stream and several polarity switches. We have compared our results with in situ data from ACE and developed several visualisation techniques to validate connectivity not only for a specific date but also for a full CR. The choice of the input magnetic map drastically affects the connectivity estimates, with global scores going from 28% global agreement to 63% in the most extreme case. The HMI and GONG maps consistently gave the best connectivity estimations, with more than 50% correct results of the full CR. For this specific period, the GONG-ADAPT maps yielded the least reliable results, with a score below 35%. This is not surprising, as we have shown before that COCONUT required parameter adjustments for these maps. However, WSO maps which showed poor coronal agreement actually provided good connectivity estimates, showing that the Heliospheric Current Sheet (HCS) location is in the end the most crucial parameter for connectivity. Consistent data over a full Carrington rotation are to be favored compared to daily.

2610.12317.title: Data Representation Matters: Optimizing Machine Learning for X-ray Source Classification by Leveraging Spatio-Spectral Information
2610.12317.abstract: Distinguishing between faint extended X-ray sources is a fundamental yet challenging task in X-ray surveys. This paper presents a benchmark comparison of convolutional neural network models for classifying simulated XMM-Newton observations of AGN and galaxy clusters, focusing on the impact of data representation and interpretability of that data. We evaluate 1D, 2D, 2D+1D, and 3D CNNs trained on distinct data representations derived from simulated XMM-Newton observations of AGN and clusters: 1D (spectral), 2D (imaging) and 3D (event cube) data. We further apply 3D-GradCAM to interpret the learned features and assess the physical basis for the model's decision making to move beyond black-box classification. Our results demonstrate that increased spectral resolution enhances classifier performance using 1D and 2D information provides a strong baseline, the integration of both domains yields significant diagnostic gains. We find that a 3D CNN architecture applied directly to spatio-spectral event cubes provides the most robust performance, with superior consistency across cross-validation folds. Interpretability analysis reveals that the 3D model autonomously learns to distinguish the diffuse thermal emission of the intracluster medium from the localized, non-thermal power-law signatures of AGN. It exploits multi-dimensional correlations that are lost in lower-dimensional projections. While the performance gain over combined 2D and 1D baselines is marginal, the 3D approach demonstrates an ability to perform implicit background characterisation. By operating directly on total photon counts within event cubes, this method bypasses the need for manual background subtraction and modelling, offering a consistent, streamlined, end-to-end pipeline for automated classification of X-ray sources in large-scale catalogues.

2610.13771.title: TeV Gamma-Ray Emission in the DA 495 Region from HAWC Observations of J1952+2924, J1954+2837, and J1958+2848
2610.13771.abstract: Previous observations of the DA 495 region, which contains the pulsar wind nebula (PWN) DA 495 and other very-high-energy (VHE; $>100~\textrm{GeV}$) gamma-ray emitters, showed inconsistent results across different VHE experiments, including differences in the measured flux of DA 495 and in the number of reported sources. Our new dedicated analysis using 3071 days of HAWC data resolves these discrepancies. We identify three extended sources, HAWC J1952+2924 (DA 495), HAWC J1954+2837, and HAWC J1958+2848, all with curved spectra, and find a hint of a fourth source. For DA 495, a multi-wavelength analysis, including our results, radio, X-ray, and other gamma-ray data, reveals that its extended emission is best described by leptonic interactions with an inferred magnetic field of $B\sim10~μ\textrm{G}$ and that hadronic components are not required. On the other hand, we interpret the other two sources, which have no confirmed counterparts, as TeV halos associated with nearby pulsars, PSR J1954+2836 and PSR J1958+2846, respectively. These results reinforce the interpretation of DA 495 as a leptonic-dominated PWN and add two candidates to the growing population of TeV halos.

2610.14179.title: Stellar discs and intermediate-mass black holes in galactic nuclei II. Fragmenting the disc and forming the S-stars in a live nuclear star cluster
2610.14179.abstract: We present direct $N$-body simulations of a stellar disc around the supermassive black hole Sgr~A*, perturbed by an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) and embedded in a live nuclear star cluster. A retrograde IMBH with $m_\bullet=2000\,M_\odot$, relative inclination $θ_\bullet=150^\circ$, and initial semi-major axis $a_\bullet=0.15$~pc breaks the disc into three disc-like components and an angular momentum filament. The stochastic torques of the cluster, together with the IMBH's inward migration, increase the angular separation between these substructures. By ${\sim}5$~Myr, their separations become comparable to those among the observed Galactic-centre young star structures. The innermost ($a\le0.04$~pc) disc stars evolve into an S-star-like population. Relaxation driven by the cluster disperses their orbital planes, excites their eccentricities and depletes the `zone of avoidance' within ${\sim}10$~Myr even without an IMBH. The IMBH further accelerates their orbital-plane reorientation. However, the most eccentric S-stars may require an additional formation channel, such as the Hills mechanism. The distinctive signatures of the IMBH are the well-separated disc components and the eccentricity excitation confined to the radial range swept by its orbit. Dynamical friction from the cluster reduces the orbital size of a $2000\,M_\odot$ IMBH initially at $0.15$~pc by more than a factor of two within $10$~Myr. Prograde IMBHs tend to align with the stellar disc, whereas a $2000\,M_\odot$ retrograde IMBH can anti-align with the radially overlapping disc stars. We also quantify how the IMBH affects the supply of stars to the loss cone and the rates of stellar tidal disruptions and binary separations.

2610.12199.title: Autocorrelation in black hole flare movies: Departures from Kerr
2610.12199.abstract: Autocorrelation in black hole movies encodes the time delays and angular separations between gravitationally lensed images, offering a means of testing the spacetime geometry. Using an orbiting hot spot in the parametrized Johannsen-Psaltis metric with a single deformation parameter, we investigate the ability of lensing-induced correlations to distinguish departures from Kerr. From ray-traced movies, we extract the slope (k) and intercept (b) of an approximately linear secondary ridge in the time-angle autocorrelation map as potential future observables. Variations in the spin and the metric deformation parameter produce distinctive trajectories in the (k,b) plane, allowing the two observables to jointly constrain both parameters when the orbital radius, observer inclination, and orbital angular velocity are specified. By varying the orbital angular velocity, we construct a Kerr reference region in the (k,b) plane, and we find that, for some low-spin configurations with negative deformation parameters, the measured slope-intercept pairs of the secondary peaks lie outside this reference region. This feature appears for sub-Keplerian, Keplerian, and super-Keplerian motion, indicating that secondary-ridge measurements from black hole flare movies have the potential to distinguish non-Kerr signatures.

2610.11983.title: Magnetic flux cancellation in a 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulation of an emerging flux tube with a non-uniform twist
2610.11983.abstract: Flux emergence is often accompanied by flux cancellation, which may drive dynamic phenomena in the solar atmosphere. We studied magnetic flux cancellation in a three-dimensional resistive magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation of an emerging flux tube with a non-uniform twist profile. We solved time-dependent resistive MHD equations to model flux emergence into a magnetised background atmosphere. We identified several cancellation sites, estimated their cancellation rates, and examined the magnetic topology and associated jet activity. The non-uniform twist produced multiple opposite photospheric polarities, leading to a complex multipolar magnetic configuration rather than a simple dipolar structure. Interactions between inner secondary magnetic patches resulted in flux cancellation of the photospheric $B_z$ along their polarity inversion line (PIL). These interactions led to the formation of concave-up loops and a cancellation rate of $1.1 \times 10^{19}$ Mx hr$^{-1}$. During cancellation, magnetic reconnection between converging opposite polarities progressively created a coherent magnetic flux rope above the cancellation region. The evolution of the rope was associated with a blowout jet, as the rope expanded and released part of its stored twist into the overlying corona. We also examined two smaller secondary cancellation events at photospheric heights. Our results highlight the role of internal flux cancellation in restructuring the magnetic field and driving blowout-jet activity in emerging regions.

2610.11242.title: Reference-Filter-Driven Transition Probabilities for IMM-Based Satellite Maneuver Detection
2610.11242.abstract: Maneuver detection of non-cooperative satellites is an essential task of space situational awareness. The interacting multiple model (IMM) filter has been applied to detect unannounced maneuvers, but the standard IMM assumes a fixed Markov transition probability matrix (TPM) that must be tuned without knowledge of the maneuver rate of the target. To avoid this tuning, adaptive-TPM approaches update the TPM online from statistics computed inside the IMM. However, these statistics already depend on the TPM through the mixing step, and this dependence forms a feedback loop. Under the dynamics mismatch of orbit tracking, the loop can keep the maneuver probability high in the absence of a maneuver or suppress its rise when a maneuver occurs. In this paper, the TPM is driven by the normalized innovation squared (NIS) of a reference coast filter that is not mixed with the IMM, and the NIS is mapped continuously to the coast-to-maneuver transition probability. The reference-driven IMM (RD-IMM) is evaluated with four space-based optical sensors tracking a geosynchronous target. RD-IMM detects small burns that the fixed-TPM IMM fails to detect, with few false declarations in maneuver-free runs, and avoids both failures of the closed-loop adaptation. Moreover, RD-IMM reduces the position error after a small in-track burn by more than 50% compared with the single-filter approaches.

2610.12051.title: On-chip filled array hyperspectral kinetic inductance detectors (FHYKID) for line intensity mapping
2610.12051.abstract: The next generation Line Intensity Mapping (LIM) experiments will require very high throughput instrumentation, and as a consequence high pixel counts focal planes. For the study of the [CII] line in the redshift range z=7-8, we develop a hyperspectral filled focal plane (FHYKID) operating in the range 210-235 GHz and with a spectral resolution reaching 120. The spectral filtering is achieved thanks to planar Slot Split Ring Resonators (SSRR) coupled to Lumped Element Kinetic Inductance Detectors (LEKID). This robust concept achieves, thanks to its simplicity, large quantum efficiency and is scalable, even with current readout electronics systems, to several tens of thousands beams on Sky. Our FHYKID will be one of the four channels of the NIKONA instrument, currently seeking funding and to be installed at the IRAM 30-meter telescope at Pico Veleta. Among the science goals, simultaneously mapping the local (galactic and nearby-galaxies) CO line and the cosmological [CII].

2610.12719.title: Stochastic gravitational waves from narrow-band cosmological magnetic fields
2610.12719.abstract: We calculate the spectrum of gravitational waves generated by a cosmological magnetic field with a narrow-band power spectrum. For a spectrum narrowly peaked at a comoving wavenumber $k_c$, we find that the gravitational wave signal peaks at $2k_c$ and has a sharp cutoff at this scale. We apply this result to an ultralight dark matter model of magnetogenesis operating around recombination, in which an axion-photon coupling generates a helical magnetic field by parametric resonance. We determine the conditions for the resulting gravitational waves to enter the frequency range of pulsar timing experiments. Although the required frequency can be reached for sufficiently large coupling, the corresponding amplitude is below the experimental sensitivity for physically allowed energy densities of the magnetic field. We generalize this conclusion to models of magnetogenesis operating at other epochs, estimating as $T \simeq 160 \mathrm{MeV}$ the temperature of a magnetogenesis process assumed to be the source of the stochastic gravitational wave background suggested by pulsar timing arrays. We place the lower bound $T \gtrsim 1$-$10 \mathrm{MeV}$ on such viable models.

2610.11095.title: Production Memory of the $^{225}\mathrm{Ra}$-$^{225}\mathrm{Ac}$ Clock in Neutron-Star Merger Ejecta
2610.11095.abstract: Radioactive nuclei in neutron-star merger ejecta carry information about both their abundance and their production history. Using the $^{225}\mathrm{Ra}$-$^{225}\mathrm{Ac}$ sequence, we establish exact conditions linking a surviving isotope partition to the time available for parent decay. An Ac fraction of 0.1 produced solely through Ra decay requires at least 2.456 days, providing a direct consistency test for proposed source states. We show that subsequent activity retains additional production memory: two histories with the same mean birth time can produce different response crossings. This distinction is captured analytically and separates mean chronology from the influence of the production-time distribution. A controlled radiation calculation then shows how deposition and photon escape transform the nuclear contrast into a common light-curve pivot for fixed ejecta properties. The results connect nuclear production chronology to late-time merger emission and provide benchmarks for nucleosynthesis and radiation-transport calculations.

2610.12356.title: A morphological search for stable year-scale modulation in gamma-ray blazars
2610.12356.abstract: Year-scale quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in blazar gamma-ray light curves have been proposed as signatures of supermassive binary black holes and precessing jets. Red noise can mimic periodicity, and detection alone does not establish persistence or period stability. We develop and calibrate a morphological framework to characterize year-scale modulation and constrain the incidence of stable modulation in blazars. We analyze 120 Fermi-LAT light curves spanning 18.1 yr. Singular spectrum analysis selects the oscillatory mode and period, while weighted wavelet Z-transform ridge tracking measures persistence, period drift, and cycle-to-cycle volatility. Flux randomization, 10,000 red-noise simulations, and about 20,000 injections calibrate the classification. Of 97 quality-selected sources, two show persistent, coherent modulation consistent with a stationary period (Rank I: PG 1553+113 and B2 1215+30), six show coherent modulation whose stationarity cannot be established (Rank II), and 89 form Rank III. Neither Rank I nor Rank II significantly exceeds red-noise expectations. Stationary 1-3 yr injections reach Rank I in 63-97% of trials at signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) = 1, depending on period, and 100% at SNR = 2; 92% of drifting injections reach Rank II. These results limit stable, approximately sinusoidal 1-3 yr modulation to at most 7% of the sample at SNR >= 1 and 5% at SNR >= 2 (95% confidence). PG 1553+113 has the lowest false-alarm probability, 4.7% after trials. Stable year-scale modulation is uncommon, and no source is established as periodic. The framework distinguishes persistent, stationary modulation from coherent variability whose period may evolve or fluctuate, but not the physical mechanism. PG 1553+113 and B2 1215+30 are candidates for monitoring and continuous gravitational-wave searches, although their stability does not establish a binary origin.

2610.12179.title: The variance of the CMB temperature gradient: a dependence on the spatial orientation and anisotropy of a multiply connected Universe
2610.12179.abstract: In the present work we develop a model--independent method to reveal the underlying patterns of anisotropy and geometry in CMB temperature maps. This method, based on the rho-statistics and a process of mask--sweeping, unveils faint but persistent geometrical and periodic structures characterising the anisotropy of the CMB in a universe with 3-torus topology. We assess that the patterns detected over large ensembles of toroidal maps match geometrically to the layouts of expected circles-in-the-sky. The mask--sweeping method explores the whole CMB over 768 mask orientations. Thus we are able to re-verify the linear relation between L the size of the cubic torus and rho the standard deviation of the normalised variance of the CMB temperature gradient. This confers a finite size s of approximately 3 Hubble lengths to our Universe with toroidal topology. Furthermore, it is shown that the violation of statistical isotropy is so faint that this has almost no influence on the linear relation between rho and L. A topology like the cubic toroidal one imposes to our Universe periodic conditions (that can be seen as periodic boundary conditions) which constrain the global degree of inhomogeneity and a zero average curvature. We demonstrate here that rho is not only a statistical signature of the spatial finiteness and size of our Universe (may its topology be simply or multiply connected) but also outlines the patterns of anisotropy of the CMB with the help of the mask--sweeping process.

2610.12298.title: Cavity Characterization for the Princeton Axion Search
2610.12298.abstract: The Princeton Axion Search (PXS) targets the mass window $0.8\text{--}2.1~μ\text{eV}$ (corresponding to frequencies $200\text{--}500~\text{MHz}$) at DFSZ sensitivity. The experiment, a haloscope, will use a cylindrical copper-plated aluminum cavity of $700~\text{mm}$ diameter and $1022~\text{mm}$ height, immersed in a $5~\text{T}$ solenoidal magnetic field. A $152~\text{mm}$ diameter tuning rod spanning the height of the cavity rotates to tune the primary mode resonance from $390\text{--}480~\text{MHz}$, the frequency range for initial operations. We deduce the electric and magnetic field mode patterns using a combination of dielectric and metallic bead perturbations on the empty cavity. The measured mode frequencies and the $\text{TM}_{010}$ field profile, as a function of tuning rod position, are in excellent agreement with simulations. We describe the effect of fabrication and assembly imperfections, including the bowing of end plates and tilt of the tuning rod. The welded seams and end-cap joints are demonstrated to not significantly degrade $Q$. We combine measurement and simulation to assess an uncertainty on form factor across the full tuning range. Our results validate PXS's cavity architecture and inform future searches for sub-$μ\text{eV}$ axions, in which large-volume high-$Q$ structures are required to reach QCD sensitivity.

2610.11616.title: Holographic dark energy from generalized entropies and extended infrared cut-offs
2610.11616.abstract: We study holographic dark energy models constructed from generalized entropy functionals and local infrared cut-offs. Three entropies (Barrow and the three and five-parameter generalized entropies) are each combined with the Granda-Oliveros (GO) cut-off and two extensions, one adding a $γH^{-2}$ term and one a $γ\ddot{H}/H$ term, the latter raising the dark-energy evolution equation to second order. The nine resulting models are constrained against DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+ and a Planck compressed CMB likelihood through an MCMC analysis, and compared using the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. The Hubble constant is stable across all models. The $H^{-2}$ term is unconstrained in every case, as it becomes relevant only in the far future, and never improves on the GO cut-off. The $\ddot{H}/H$ term, instead, is tightly constrained for Barrow and $S_5$, where it improves the fit substantially, but not for $S_3$. The best fit is obtained for Barrow entropy with the $\ddot{H}/H$ cut-off, yet the Barrow exponent remains compatible with zero in all cases. The data thus favour a higher-order infrared cut-off, while showing no significant evidence for a departure from the Bekenstein-Hawking area law. We also investigate the dark energy equation of state (EoS) of $S_3$ and $S_5$, discovering quintessence-like behavior and phantom crossing.

2610.13223.title: Combination of multi-observatory photometry to determine asteroid rotation periods
2610.13223.abstract: This study aims to determine asteroid rotation periods from sparse, unevenly sampled, multi-observatory photometry using the Lomb-Scargle (L-S) method. The photometric measurements of the asteroids are taken from the circulars of the Minor Planet Center (MPC). Twelve asteroids, four of them with known rotation periods, were analyzed with two complementary methods. In the separate dataset analysis (S-method), each observatory dataset was analyzed separately, and the final period was obtained as a weighted average of the consistent candidate periods, with weights based on the peak power of the power spectrum, the number of measurements, and the quality of the corresponding light curve fit. In the combined dataset analysis (C-method), all measurements were corrected for the biases of the photometric band, the star catalog and the observatory, reduced to a common scale and merged into a single dataset, after which the period was derived directly from the L-S analysis of the combined time series. Both methods produced consistent results, and they reproduced the known periods of the four test asteroids within 0.05%. The results show that the L-S method is well suited for finding rotation periods in sparse observations with uneven sampling over long time intervals. New rotation periods were found for asteroids 2968, 2971, 3081, 3473, 3716, and 4303. The period of 2968 remains ambiguous because of daily aliasing. For 3716, the most likely period is 10.474 hours, but its daily alias at 13.405 hours cannot be excluded completely. For 3173, the strongest peaks at 22.99 and 45.98 hours are probably daily aliases of a slower brightness variation. For asteroid 2607, the period agrees with a recently published value and is more precise. The approach is therefore promising for automated searches for unknown asteroid rotation periods.

2610.13537.title: First Experimental Results of Space Object Detection Using the InteRFeX Array
2610.13537.abstract: This paper presents the first experimental validation of InteRFeX, a non-uniform receive only (passive) array located at the Nova Systems Space Precinct in Peterborough, Australia, designed for space domain awareness applications. It operates over a frequency range of 70 to 300 MHz and is capable of functioning in a range of observational modes, including as a coherent passive bistatic radar for space surveillance, which is the focus of this work. InteRFeX exploits commercial broadcast transmissions as illuminators of opportunity, combining cross-ambiguity function processing for bistatic range and range-rate retrieval with MUSIC-based direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation for angular localization. The International Space Station (ISS) serves as the experimental target, with measurements evaluated against Two-Line Element (TLE) orbit predictions. Taking advantage of the dual-polarized array, all four reference--surveillance polarization combinations are evaluated, revealing differences in detection rate and mean signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) over the observation pass, with bistatic-range RMSEs of approximately 1 km relative to the TLE-derived reference. Independently, the MUSIC-based DoA estimates exhibit a mean angular separation of approximately $0.45^\circ$ from the TLE-derived reference directions. The angular deviations are further decomposed into along-track and cross-track components, enabling a more detailed characterization of the DoA offsets relative to the TLE-derived reference trajectory. The processing framework also includes a first-order bistatic link-budget analysis to estimate the expected SNR over the observation geometry. These results demonstrate the feasibility of passive-radar space domain awareness using radio-interferometric array technology and establish the proposed signal-processing pipeline as a basis for a dedicated coherent passive-radar mode within InteRFeX.

2610.12889.title: Direct detection constraints on EFT operators for inelastic dark matter
2610.12889.abstract: We convert existing exclusion limits on the elastic spin-independent (SI) dark matter--proton cross sections into upper bounds on the event rate, subsequently applying them to constrain other effective operators for inelastic scattering of light dark matter in the GeV mass region. We focus on three representative scenarios including the isoscalar, proton-philic, and the proton-philic spin-dependent inelastic dark matter model, which are well-motivated in phenomenological studies of dark matter detection.

2610.13774.title: Insights from the stability of methanol maser flare properties I: G9.62+0.20E
2610.13774.abstract: The brightest 6.7 GHz methanol maser in the Galaxy is associated with the high-mass star-forming region (HMSFR) G009.62+0.20E. Additionally, this methanol maser shows periodic flaring observed at 6.7 and 12.2 GHz. Several models have been hypothesized to explain the periodicity, including periodic accretion, spiral shocks in the gaps of circumbinary disks, pulsating stars, dicke's superradiance, and a colliding wind binary (CWB) system. We analyzed the time series of the 1.22 km s-1 feature of the 6.7 GHz methanol maser spectrum and the 1.25 km s-1 feature of the 12.2 GHz methanol maser spectrum over the monitoring duration of roughly 20 years, to determine an updated period, analyze the stability and repeatability of the flares, the temporal behavior of the flare profile, and the duty cycle of the flare profile based on the updated period. From these results, it is argued for or against any of the mechanisms that have been proposed to explain the periodicity. Lomb-Scargle (LS) and phase dispersion minimization (PDM) methods were used to determine the methanol maser period at 6.7 and 12.2 GHz. Once the period has been determined, phase-folding or period-folding was used to analyze the flare shape, flare stability, and duty cycle of the flares. The periods of the 6.7 and 12.2 GHz methanol masers were determined to be ~ 243.0 +- 0.3 days. The flares are highly repeatable, stable, and show almost identical shapes, as well as their duty cycles. A replicated kernel density estimator (KDE) of the flare shape reproduces the time series very well over a time span of ~ 8000 days. After careful consideration of the proposed mechanisms for periodic methanol masers, we conclude that all but one, the CWB model, have been ruled out as a possible driver of this flare profile. It has also been established that the CWB model can qualitatively explain the flare profile of the periodic methanol masers.

2610.12043.title: Volume Dependence of Helicity-based Eruption Diagnostics in Recurrent Coronal Jets
2610.12043.abstract: Recurrent solar coronal jets originate from the same source region, providing a useful setting for studying the buildup, redistribution, and release of magnetic energy and helicity. However, how these quantities can characterize magnetic evolution and the onset conditions of the eruptions remains unclear. We perform a full three-dimensional (3D) thermodynamic magnetohydrodynamic simulation of recurrent jets driven by converging motions imposed at the bottom boundary. The simulation naturally produces two successive eruptions. The current-carrying helicity $H_J$ decreases during the first jet and gradually recovers between the two jets. In contrast, the free magnetic energy $E_{\mathrm{free}}$ shows no clear accumulation after its first release. This difference indicates that $H_J$ provides information on magnetic evolution beyond that provided by $E_{\mathrm{free}}$. Furthermore, the commonly used helicity ratio $H_J/H_V$ reaches different peaks near the onset of the two jets and is sensitive to the integration volume. By comparison, the locally normalized quantity $H_J/Φ_{\mathrm{closed}}^2$ reaches similar peaks near the onset of both jets and is relatively insensitive to the choice among the tested integration volumes, where $Φ_{\mathrm{closed}}$ is the single-polarity magnetic flux of the closed-field domain. These results reveal the local nature of the eruptions and suggest that $H_J$ normalized by the square of the closed magnetic flux may be a useful diagnostic of eruptive conditions.

2610.12943.title: In-flight Timing Calibration of the Follow-up X-Ray Telescope on Board the Einstein Probe
2610.12943.abstract: After the launch of Einstein Probe (EP), pulsars are observed to calibrate the timing system of the onboard Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT) by measuring the times of arrival (TOAs). FXT has two independently operating modules, namely FXTA and FXTB, each equipped with the Wolter-I optics and the pnCCD camera. For scientific observations, each pnCCD has three distinct readout modes that differ in frame cycles, the full frame mode (FF, 50 ms per frame), the partial windowed mode (PW, 2.2 ms per frame), and the timing mode (TM, 23.68 $μ$s per row, 9.4352 ms per frame). Thus, 1RXS J170849.0--400910 with the spin period of 11 s is observed in FF, PSR B1509--58 (150 ms) in PW, and Crab pulsar (33 ms) in TM as well as PSR B1821--24 (3.05 ms) and PSR B1937+21 (1.56 ms). The TOAs of these pulsars measured by FXTA and FXTB are compared with the results of NICER, and for Crab pulsar with the Jodrell Bank Monthly Ephemeris (JBE). Results verify that the timing system of FXTA and FXTB in FF, PW, and TM modes are consistent with each other, and are in good alignment with NICER. The measured advance of the Crab pulsar's main peak relative to JBE is $357^{\pm14(stat)}_{\pm54(sys)} μ$s in FXTA and $394^{\pm14(stat)}_{\pm67(sys)} μ$s in FXTB. Based on measurements of PSR B1821--24 and PSR B1937+21, the preliminary absolute timing accuracy is estimated to be 6 $μ$s for FXTA and 31 $μ$s for FXTB in TM mode. Additionally, the systematic delay of FXTA timing results relative to FXTB is found to be $20^{\pm19(stat)}_{\pm21(sys)} μ$s.

2610.11832.title: Investigating the nature of magnetic turbulence in Tycho's SNR using X-ray observation
2610.11832.abstract: Supernova remnants (SNRs) are widely regarded as the primary sources of Galactic cosmic ray acceleration and the particles are energized at the shock front of SNRs through the diffusive shock acceleration (DSA) mechanism, gaining energy by repeatedly crossing the shock. Magnetic turbulence plays a crucial role in scattering these particles back and forth, making the investigation of turbulence essential to understanding the acceleration process. In this study, we apply the two-point correlation method to derive the magnetic energy spectrum from the non-thermal X-ray flux image of Tycho's SNR. This image was obtained using Poissonian-based Generalized Morphological Component Analysis (pGMCA). The turbulence length scale observed in the resulting spectrum is shorter than the turbulence scale derived from previous studies of radio observations of Tycho's SNR. Additionally, we use the X-ray rim thickness measured across Tycho which is an indicator of magnetic field strength to estimate the magnetic energy spectrum. The turbulence scale inferred from this method is consistent with that obtained from the non-thermal X-ray flux analysis.

2610.13173.title: Formation Dynamics of a Rotating Solar Spicule-like Event and Associated Energy-Mass Transport
2610.13173.abstract: We performed three-dimensional radiative magnetohydrodynamic(3D RMHD) simulations in an upward-directed (positive-polarity) open magnetic field with an initial background strength of 10 G. We identified vortex-associated spicule-like events and carried out a detailed analysis of one representative event. Prior to the formation of this spicule-like event, a photospheric vortex appears and twists the magnetic field lines, then develops upward into higher atmospheric layers, forming a magnetic tornado system. This event is generated during this process. At the periphery of this magnetic tornado, twisted magnetic field lines with negative vertical components reconnect with both external positive-polarity background fields and central positive-polarity fields. The magnetic reconnection sites rise and rotate together with the developed magnetic tornado, and many jet-like substructures in this event are closely associated with plasma upward ejections from these reconnection regions. A vertical force analysis shows that, for this event, plasma uplift in the photosphere and lower chromosphere is dominated by the pressure-gradient force, whereas in the upper chromosphere, the Lorentz force gradually becomes dominant. At a height of about 4 Mm above the solar surface, this event produces a mean upward mass flux density on the order of $10^{-7}~{\rm kg~m^{-2}~s^{-1}}$ and a mean upward Poynting flux density of approximately $525~{\rm W~m^{-2}}$. The wave-mode decomposition results show that the energy transport associated with the rotational spicule-like event is dominated by the Alfvén mode. Alfvén waves, fast-mode waves, and slow-mode waves carry energy into the lower corona in an approximate ratio of $10:7:3$.

2610.11127.title: Improved analysis of time delays between radio wavelengths and X-ray of Sgr A* flares in the shock oscillation model
2610.11127.abstract: We present an improved analysis of the time delays between radio and X-ray flares from the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), extending our previous shock oscillation model by incorporating Compton scattering. Our simulations predict delay times of 1-4 h between X-ray and radio flares, 20-40 min and 0.5-1 h between 334 GHz and 4.5 $μ$m and 2-8 keV flares, and 7-20 min and 0.5-1 h between 22-43 GHz and 350 GHz radio flares, respectively, in good agreement with recent observations. The delay time between the radio emissions (synchrotron) and X-ray emissions (bremsstrahlung) is interpreted as the transit time for sound waves traveling from the central core near the event horizon to the location of the oscillating shock. Additionally, the delay time observed between different radio wavelengths corresponds to the transit time of sound waves moving between the frequency-dependent effective radii $R_{\rm eff}(ν)$, where the optical thickness $τ_ν(R)$ at frequency $ν$ equals one on the surface of the accretion disc. The X-ray emission and the radio emission at lower frequencies peak later than the radio emission at higher frequencies. This delay occurs because the acoustic perturbations created by synchrotron emission peak near the event horizon and then expand outward. Conversely, an inverse delay happens when the acoustic waves generated by the upstream shock wave travel toward the event horizon. The predicted delay times from this interpretation qualitatively match the numerical results obtained in simulations.

2610.12974.title: An Ultraviolet Instrument on the Habitable Worlds Observatory: Considerations and Capability Trades on the Multi-Object, Integral-field, and High-resolution modes of a potential UVI
2610.12974.abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) is NASA's next-generation astrophysics platform, delivering transformative capability in the search for life and study of the origins of the universe. Amongst the instruments under consideration for HWO is a multi-purpose ultraviolet spectrograph and imager that provides a deep toolbox for some of the most pressing science investigations of the next several decades. In this paper, we present a basic draft model of a potential UVI, including a multi-object spectrograph, far ultraviolet imager, high resolution spectrograph, and integral-field spectrograph. The draft designs for these channels of the UV instrument serve as a basis for a general discussion of the instrument architecture and design challenges, while also identifying potential trades, enhancements, and other considerations that the HWO project will need to address as it moves into the formulation phase. We conclude with a presentation of several scientific simulations that have helped guide the capabilities of the draft design. This paper is intended to serve as a summary of UV instrument modes, technology, and potential design ahead of planned instrument studies in the late 2020's, and then Phase A in the early 2030's.

2610.13514.title: The School on Gravity: from motion to commotion
2610.13514.abstract: Understanding the gravitational interaction is one of the great scientific endeavors of the 21st century. The Nobel Prize-winning discovery of gravitational waves in 2015, and subsequent detections by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration, have marked a revolutionary step forward in physics and astrophysics by opening an entirely new window for exploring the Universe. Future upgrades to these detectors, along with upcoming facilities such as LISA, the Einstein Telescope, and radio and optical instruments, promise other breakthrough discoveries that the next generation of scientists will need to interpret. The School on Gravity (22--26 June 2026, Copenhagen) aimed to introduce junior scientists--graduate students and advanced undergraduates with a background in general relativity--to a wide range of foundational topics in the exciting new field of gravitational-wave physics. Topics spanned from the theory of motion, to new challenges introduced by quantum physics, to the astrophysics of black holes and source modeling for gravitational-wave detectors. The School on Gravity took place at the legendary Auditorium A of the Niels Bohr Institute, inviting students and lecturers to challenge current paradigms in gravitational physics in the spirit of the quantum revolution that unfolded in this very room. These lecture notes aim at opening up those new ideas presented in Auditorium A to the rest of the scientific community.

2610.11637.title: Gravitational Microlensing
2610.11637.abstract: Gravitational microlensing is a unique planet-detection method that does not rely on detecting light from the host star or planet. Instead, planets are discovered when their gravitational field perturbs the light coming from a distant source. The mechanics of this method offer several advantages. It has the ability to detect wide-orbit planets of various masses around host stars of different types, at and beyond the system's snow line. Thus, microlensing complements the other detecting techniques that are more sensitive to close-orbit or high-mass planets. In this Chapter, we review the microlensing method and discuss how the physical properties, such as mass and distance, can be extracted from the microlensing light curve or from additional high-angular resolution observations. Microlensing is essential for the broader context of exoplanet demographics, as it can place constraints on planets, in wide orbits, beyond the {\it snow line}. Studying this parameter space can help us unravel the details of planet formation and how our own Solar System formed. Lastly, we provide an example of how to model a light curve and obtain accurate physical parameters for the host and planet.
